reasons: 화풍: 윤곽이 근흑(재질 어두운 톤 아님) (4/4)

surfaces.part: 4x4 grid of shoe cubby doors (front face)

answer.evidence: Rows 1-4 form a top band that brightens from tan to a pale 1-row front-edge line at row 4. Row 5 is a dark eave shadow line, and the vertical front face runs below it. The front face (rows 6-30) is a 4x4 grid of cubby doors separated by dark bars at rows 11, 17 and 23, with a base at rows 29-30. The top band is 4 rows, thicker than a 1-2 row rim and comparable to the green cabinet reference (top surface, edge line, eave shadow). There is no side face, so this is a front-facing 3/4 view.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tan wooden grid of cubbies inside a dark frame. It has about 4 lightness steps on the wood: a light face, a mid tone, a dark slot interior and the frame. The references use 5-6 steps per material. The measured dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, so the outline is a uniform near-black line around the whole piece and every cubby. That is the 'sticker' look. The references with tinted edges (hedge 0%, cheese stall 1%) show the Beodeul practice of using the dark tone of the adjacent material. Visible tones per tile are 10 against 9 for the hedge, 17 for the cheese stall and 20 for the well, so density is only comparable to the simplest reference. Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no big flat fills, but the compartments repeat identically with little per-plank grain, wear or per-slot highlight. A careful artist would not accept it next to the well and the stall because it reads flatter and more outlined.

answer.evidence: Rows 1-4 form a band at the top, shaded from dark to light, and it ends in a dark front-edge line at row 5 (L=44, darker than both neighbours). That line works as the edge and eave shadow, so the band counts as a thin top surface of about 4 rows. Below it, rows 6-28 are the front face: a face-on 4x4 grid of compartments, each with a bevel and a dark knob. Rows 29-30 are a plinth. The top is thin but has an edge line and shadow, so it is more than a bare rim. The front face is about 25 rows. No side face is drawn. The call is borderline, since the top band could also be read as a gradient cornice.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tan grid of identical locker cells with a dark frame. It has about 4 lightness steps on the wood: a light face, a mid tone, a dark cell recess and a dark frame. The well and the cheese stall have 6 or more steps plus per-element highlights. The measured dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, which points to a uniform dark, barely tinted line around the frame and every cell. That is the sticker look, not the adjacent-material dark tone the references use (hedge 0%, stall 1%). Texture is limited to slight panel shading, with no visible grain, no per-board variation and no wear dots. The measured 10 visible tones per tile is on par with the hedge but well below the well (20) and stall (17). The repeated cells are very regular and mechanical, so the piece reads thinner and flatter than the references. A careful artist would not accept it next to the well or stall without more shading steps and tinted outlines.

answer.evidence: Rows 1-4 form a top band that gets lighter downward and ends in the lightest row (row 4) as a front-edge line. Row 5 is a dark eave shadow under it. Below that, rows 6-28 are a 4x4 grid of square cubby fronts and rows 29-31 are the base, giving a front face of about 26 rows. The top band is only 4 rows and has a weak depth cue, since its gradient could also be read as a front-facing cornice. The edge line plus eave shadow still count as evidence (a). No side face is drawn.

styleAnswer.evidence: The locker is a regular grid of tan cubbies in a dark frame. Each cubby has only about 2-3 tan steps (light face, slightly darker inner shadow), and the frame is a single dark tone. The measured 100% near-neutral dark edge pixels matches the grey-black sticker outline. The references use outlines tinted to the material: the hedge is 0% neutral, the stall 1%, the well 33%. The 10 visible tones per tile and 0% near-flat coverage keep it above the weakest references, so no large flat fills. But it falls well short of the stall (17 tones) and well (20 tones). The cubbies are repeated identically, with no wood grain, no per-slot shading variation and no highlight/shadow ramp on the frame. By eye it looks flatter and more sticker-like than the same-scale references, so I fail it.

answer.evidence: Rows 1-4 form a top band that brightens from a dark outline-adjacent row 1 (L=103) up to the lightest row 4 (L=203). Row 4 is a light front-edge line, and row 5 is a dark eave shadow (L=44). Below it, rows 6-29 are the front face, a 4x4 grid of locker doors separated by dark dividers at rows 11, 17 and 23. The silhouette is a constant 30 px wide, so no side face is drawn. The top band is thin at 4 rows, but it has an edge line and a shadow, so it counts as a top surface rather than a plain rim.

styleAnswer.evidence: The locker is a tan grid of cubbyholes in a darker frame. The whole piece uses only 10 distinct colours, against 38-40 for the stall and well. Its wood ramp has about 4 steps, with little per-plank grain or per-cubby variation, where the references use 5-6. The measured near-neutral share of dark edge pixels is 100%, so the outline reads as a neutral dark line, not a dark brown version of the wood, which is the sticker look. At 10 visible tones per tile it roughly matches the hedge (9), but it is well below the stall (17) and well (20). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no true flat fills, though the cubby interiors look fairly uniform to the eye. Overall it is shallower and more sticker-like than the references, so it fails.
